title: Firewalls & VPN
subtitle: Four firewall generations, ACL grammar, DMZ/NAT architecture, IPsec & SSL VPN modes

readingSections.title: What a Firewall Actually Does
readingSections.quickSummary: A policy-enforcement point between trust zones: permits, denies, logs and alerts traffic based on organisation-defined rules.
content: A firewall is a network security device (hardware, software, or both) that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing traffic according to security RULES the organisation defines. It is the barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks - the choke point where policy becomes enforcement.

Four core actions: PERMIT (allow matching traffic), DENY (silently drop), REJECT (drop and tell the sender), and LOG (record for audit). Rules evaluate in order - typically top-down, first-match-wins - ending in an implicit 'deny all' default on hardened systems.

Firewalls live at trust boundaries: Internet edge (perimeter), between internal segments (internal segmentation), and on hosts (personal/host-based firewalls). Placement questions test which boundary a description implies.

subsections.title: Rule anatomy
subsections.content: A rule names: source IP, destination IP, protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP), source/destination PORT, and the ACTION. Example: 'permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp' - the published AXIS ACL question is exactly this grammar.

subsections.title: Default stance
subsections.content: Default deny (everything blocked unless permitted) is the secure stance; default allow is convenience-first. Exams frame 'most secure configuration' - the answer is default-deny with explicit permits.

quickRevision: Firewall = policy enforcement at a trust boundary.
Rules: source, destination, protocol, port, action.
tricks: ACL grammar questions map directly: access-list NUMBER ACTION PROTOCOL SOURCE DEST eq PORT.
Standard ACL (1-99) filters by SOURCE only; extended (100-199) adds protocol + destination + port - the published PYQ hinged on this.
'Reject' vs 'deny': reject replies (faster failure for users); deny stays silent (harder to scan).
patterns: 'Barrier between private network and Internet' - the definition stem.
'Which rule permits mail to only one host?' - extended ACL with eq smtp.

pyqPatterns.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
pyqPatterns.question: What command will permit SMTP mail to only host 1.1.1.1?
pyqPatterns.approach: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp - extended ACL, tcp protocol, destination port smtp.

readingSections.companyNote: Cisco-flavoured ACL questions appear verbatim in published AXIS sets - one grammar, three question variants.

readingSections.title: The Four Firewall Generations
readingSections.quickSummary: Packet filter (headers) -> Proxy (application messages) -> Stateful (active connections) -> NGFW (deep packet inspection + app awareness).
content: Generation 1 - PACKET FILTERING: the first-generation firewall inspects small amounts of data - packet headers (source/destination IP, ports, protocol) - and permits or denies per filter standards. Fast and cheap, but blind to payload and to whether a packet belongs to an existing conversation. Implemented as router ACLs.

Generation 2 - PROXY SERVICE (application-level gateways): an intermediary stands between client and server, filtering messages at the APPLICATION layer. The proxy terminates each connection and re-originates it - real content awareness, but slower and per-protocol.

Generation 3 - STATEFUL INSPECTION: dynamic packet filtering that tracks ACTIVE connections in a state table. Packets belonging to established, legitimate sessions pass without explicit rules; unsolicited packets are dropped. The phrase 'monitors active connections' is its exam signature.

Generation 4 - NEXT-GENERATION FIREWALL (NGFW): deep packet inspection (full payload, not just headers) plus application-level identification, user-identity awareness, and integrated IPS. 'Deep packet inspection with application-level inspection' is the published definition.

subsections.title: The inspection ladder
subsections.content: Headers (packet filter) -> full messages (proxy) -> connection context (stateful) -> payload + identity (NGFW). Each generation answers one question the previous could not: 'is this packet FROM a real conversation?' (stateful) and 'what application is this really?' (NGFW).

quickRevision: 4: NGFW - deep packet inspection + app awareness.
tricks: Signature phrases map 1:1: 'headers' -> packet filter; 'application layer' -> proxy; 'active connections' -> stateful; 'deep packet inspection' -> NGFW.
Stateful vs packet filter: only stateful knows a reply packet belongs to an existing session.
NGFW vs proxy: both see content, but NGFW inspects inline at wire speed with IPS integration.
patterns: 'Filters messages at the application layer' -> proxy service.
'Deep packet inspection with application-level inspection' -> NGFW.

pyqPatterns.question: Match firewall type to description (all four generations).
pyqPatterns.approach: The four syllabus definitions are quoted word-for-word in options - memorise the signature phrases.

readingSections.companyNote: All four generation definitions come straight from the official PrepInsta syllabus page - the highest-yield memorisation in this topic.

readingSections.title: DMZ, NAT & Firewall Architecture
readingSections.quickSummary: A DMZ hosts public-facing servers between two firewall legs; NAT hides internal addresses; bastion hosts and screened subnets are the classic layouts.
content: A DMZ (demilitarised zone) is a buffer subnetwork hosting PUBLIC-FACING servers (web, mail, DNS) so a compromise there cannot reach the internal LAN directly. Classic layouts: three-legged firewall (one box, three interfaces: LAN/WAN/DMZ) and screened subnet (two firewalls sandwiching the DMZ).
A bastion host is the hardened, exposed server that faces the Internet - nothing else runs on it. A screening router is the packet-filter at the edge.

NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites private source addresses to the public IP at the gateway - hiding internal topology and letting many hosts share one public IP (PAT/NAT overload). NAT is not a firewall, but it obscures internal addressing, which helps.
Egress vs ingress filtering: ingress filters incoming traffic; egress filters OUTGOING traffic (stopping compromised machines from attacking others or leaking data).

subsections.title: Layout comparison
subsections.content:
Screened router - one packet-filter at the edge (weakest).
Screened host - router + bastion host inside.
Three-legged (DMZ on a third interface) - one device, three zones.
Screened subnet - two firewalls, DMZ sandwiched (strongest classic design).

quickRevision: DMZ = buffer zone for public servers.
NAT hides internal addresses (not a security control by itself).
tricks: 'Public web server placed safely' -> DMZ, never the LAN.
Two firewalls sandwiching servers = screened subnet; one device with three legs = three-legged.
Egress vs ingress: OUT-going vs IN-coming filtering.
patterns: 'Buffer network between internal and Internet' - DMZ.
'Many private hosts share one public IP' - NAT/PAT.

pyqPatterns.question: Where should a public web server be placed?
pyqPatterns.approach: DMZ - isolated from the internal LAN.

readingSections.companyNote: DMZ placement is a recurring one-mark question across placement papers.

readingSections.title: VPN Protocols, Modes & Use Cases
readingSections.quickSummary: VPNs build encrypted tunnels over public networks: IPsec (site-to-site, network layer) vs SSL/TLS VPN (remote access, browser-friendly); tunnel vs transport modes.
content: A Virtual Private Network extends a private network across a public one by wrapping traffic in an ENCRYPTED TUNNEL: confidentiality (nobody reads it), integrity (nobody alters it undetected), and authentication (both ends prove identity).

Two protocol families dominate. IPSEC operates at the network layer - the standard for SITE-TO-SITE links (office-to-office) with two modes: TUNNEL mode (encrypts the whole original IP packet, adds a new header - gateway-to-gateway) and TRANSPORT mode (encrypts only the payload - host-to-host). Components: AH (authentication header - integrity/auth), ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload - encryption + integrity), IKE (Internet Key Exchange - negotiates keys).

SSL/TLS VPN operates at the session/application layer - the REMOTE-ACCESS favourite because it needs no client software beyond a browser and filters through firewalls easily (it looks like HTTPS on 443). WireGuard and OpenVPN are modern open implementations.

Use cases: remote workers, branch-office site-to-site, securing public Wi-Fi, bypassing geo-restrictions (consumer framing). What a VPN does NOT do: stop malware, replace the firewall's filtering, or make you anonymous from your VPN provider.

subsections.title: Tunnel vs transport
subsections.content:
Tunnel mode: entire original IP packet encrypted + new IP header -> gateways/site-to-site.
Transport mode: payload encrypted, original IP header intact -> end-to-end host communication.

quickRevision: VPN = encrypted tunnel: confidentiality + integrity + authentication.
IPsec = network layer, site-to-site; ESP encrypts, AH authenticates, IKE negotiates.
Tunnel mode = whole packet; transport mode = payload only.
tricks: 'Site-to-site office link' -> IPsec tunnel mode; 'road warrior with a laptop' -> SSL VPN.
ESP encrypts; AH only authenticates - ESP+AH = the full IPsec suite.
VPN questions pair with MITM: the tunnel is the anti-interception answer.
patterns: 'Encrypted tunnel over public network' - VPN definition.
'Secure remote access from anywhere' - SSL/TLS VPN.

pyqPatterns.question: Which network security ensures attackers cannot infiltrate your network? (options included VPN)
pyqPatterns.approach: The published answer keyed VPN - read carefully: standard doctrine credits the FIREWALL with infiltration prevention; VPN adds encrypted remote access. Know both framings.

readingSections.companyNote: VPN questions in published sets lean conceptual (tunnel, remote access) - IPsec component trivia (AH/ESP/IKE) is the stretch material.

formulas.title: ACL Grammar (Cisco-style)

formula.latex: \text{access-list } \langle n \rangle \; \text{action protocol src dest eq port}
formula.text: Standard ACLs 1-99 filter by source; extended 100-199 add protocol, destination and port.

formulas.whenToUse: Every Cisco-flavoured ACL question in the AXIS pool.
explanation: Standard: access-list 10 deny 172.16.48.0 0.0.15.255 - source + wildcard only.
Extended: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp - protocol + port.
Wildcard = inverse mask: /20 -> 0.0.15.255.
Implicit deny all at the end of every ACL.

steps: Extended list 110: permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp.
example.answer: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp

formulas.commonMistake: Using a standard ACL to filter ports - impossible by definition.

formulas.title: Firewall Generation Ladder

formula.text: Packet filter -> proxy -> stateful -> NGFW; each generation inspects one level deeper.

explanation: Packet filter: header fields only; router ACLs.
Proxy: application-layer intermediary; per-protocol.
Stateful: connection state table; dynamic packet filtering.
NGFW: DPI + application identity + user awareness + IPS.

example.prompt: Tracks active connections to permit replies.

formulas.commonMistake: Calling stateful 'application layer' - that phrase belongs to proxy.

formulas.title: Stateful Logic

formula.text: Outbound connections create state entries; only replies to established sessions pass inbound.

formulas.whenToUse: 'How does the firewall know this reply is legitimate?' questions.
explanation: Outbound SYN creates a table entry (src, dst, ports, seq).
Inbound packets are matched against the table.
No matching session -> dropped, even if rules would allow it.
State exhaustion is a DoS vector (SYN floods).

example.prompt: Why did the unsolicited inbound packet drop despite an allow rule?
steps: Stateful default: no session, no pass.
example.answer: No established session in the state table

formulas.memoryTip: No session, no entry, no entry, no pass.
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming allow rules bypass state checking.

formulas.title: DMZ Layout Selection

formula.text: From weakest to strongest classic perimeter designs.

explanation: Screened router: single packet filter - weakest.
Screened host: router + bastion host.
Three-legged: one firewall, LAN/WAN/DMZ interfaces.
Screened subnet: two firewalls sandwich the DMZ - strongest classic.

example.prompt: Public web + mail servers isolated from LAN with two firewalls.

formulas.memoryTip: More boxes between WAN and LAN = stronger.
formulas.commonMistake: Placing public servers on the LAN 'behind the firewall' - that is what the DMZ exists to avoid.

formulas.title: IPsec Modes & Components

formula.text: Tunnel mode for gateways, transport for hosts; ESP encrypts, AH authenticates, IKE negotiates keys.

explanation: Tunnel mode: new IP header wraps encrypted original - site-to-site gateways.
Transport mode: original header intact - host-to-host.
ESP: encryption + integrity + authentication.
AH: authentication + integrity only (no encryption).
IKE: negotiates keys/SAs (Security Associations).
formulas.memoryTip: Tunnel = wrapped parcel; transport = padded envelope.
formulas.commonMistake: AH encrypting - AH authenticates only; ESP encrypts.

formulas.title: VPN Protocol Map

formula.text: Pick the family by use case: gateway links vs road warriors.

explanation: IPsec: network layer; site-to-site; requires client/config.
SSL/TLS VPN: session/application layer; browser-based remote access; traverses firewalls on 443.
OpenVPN: open-source, TLS-based, flexible ports.
WireGuard: modern, minimal codebase, fast cryptography.
PPTP: legacy, broken - appears only as the 'insecure option'.

example.prompt: Remote employee with just a browser needs internal apps.

formulas.commonMistake: PPTP as a secure option - it is the deprecated wrong answer.

mcqs.q: A firewall is best defined as:
opts: A device that speeds up traffic
A barrier filtering traffic between networks per security rules
exp: Monitors and filters incoming/outgoing traffic against organisation-defined rules.

mcqs.q: Which firewall inspects packet HEADERS against filter standards?
exp: Generation 1: header fields only - fast, no payload or connection awareness.

mcqs.q: Which firewall filters messages at the APPLICATION layer?
exp: Proxy = application-level intermediary between client and server.

mcqs.q: Which firewall uses DYNAMIC packet filtering by monitoring ACTIVE connections?
exp: Stateful = the connection state table - 'active connections' is its signature phrase.

mcqs.q: NGFW is defined by:
opts: Deep packet inspection with application-level awareness
exp: Generation 4: full payload inspection + application/user identity + integrated IPS.

mcqs.q: A VPN primarily provides:
opts: An encrypted tunnel over a public network
exp: Tunnel = confidentiality + integrity + authentication across untrusted networks.

mcqs.q: Which VPN family suits OFFICE-TO-OFFICE site-to-site links?
exp: IPsec at the network layer is the site-to-site standard (tunnel mode).

mcqs.q: Which VPN suits a remote employee using only a BROWSER?
exp: SSL/TLS VPN = browser-based remote access, no client install.

mcqs.q: IPsec TUNNEL mode encrypts:
opts: The entire original IP packet (with a new header)
exp: Tunnel wraps the whole packet for gateway-to-gateway links.
Transport mode encrypts just the payload.

mcqs.q: The public-facing buffer network hosting web/mail servers is the:
exp: DMZ isolates public servers so their compromise cannot reach the LAN directly.

mcqs.q: Which IPsec component ENCRYPTS?
exp: ESP = Encapsulating Security Payload (encryption + integrity).
AH authenticates only; IKE negotiates keys.

mcqs.q: The implicit rule at the end of a hardened firewall's ACL is:
exp: Default deny - anything not explicitly permitted is dropped.

mcqs.q: A hardened, minimal server exposed to the Internet is a:
exp: Bastion = the deliberately exposed, stripped-down fortress host.

mcqs.q: NAT's security side-effect is:
opts: Hiding internal IP addresses from outsiders
exp: NAT obscures internal topology - helpful, but not a security control.

mcqs.q: Filtering OUTBOUND traffic to stop compromised machines attacking others is:
exp: Egress = exit; stops data exfiltration and outbound attacks.

mcqs.q: Which firewall would identify an application tunnelled over port 80?
exp: Port 80 carrying non-HTTP traffic is exactly what DPI/application awareness exposes.

mcqs.q: IPsec TRANSPORT mode encrypts:
exp: Transport = host-to-host payload protection; tunnel = whole packet for gateways.

mcqs.q: Which IPsec component AUTHENTICATES but does NOT encrypt?
exp: Authentication Header = integrity + origin auth; ESP carries the encryption.

mcqs.q: IKE's job in IPsec is:
exp: Internet Key Exchange sets up the SAs both gateways use.

mcqs.q: An ACL line 'access-list 10 deny 172.16.48.0 0.0.15.255' is:
opts: A standard ACL denying a /20 subnet
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Number 10 = standard range (1-99), source + wildcard only - the published PYQ answer.

mcqs.q: Permitting SMTP only to host 1.1.1.1 requires which line?
opts: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Extended ACL (100-199): tcp protocol + destination port eq smtp.

mcqs.q: Which firewall limitation does STATEFUL inspection fix?
opts: Packet filters cannot tell replies to established sessions from new attacks
exp: The state table gives connection context that header-only filters lack.

mcqs.q: A three-legged firewall has interfaces for:
exp: One device, three zones - the single-box DMZ design.

mcqs.q: Which VPN protocol is LEGACY and INSECURE?
exp: PPTP's encryption is broken - it appears only as the wrong answer.

mcqs.q: A screened subnet architecture uses:
exp: Two devices, DMZ between - the strongest classic perimeter.

mcqs.q: Which traffic would a STATEFUL firewall drop even if a generic allow rule exists?
opts: An unsolicited inbound packet with no matching session
A reply to an outbound request
exp: No session entry -> no pass, regardless of generic rules.

mcqs.q: WireGuard's selling points are:
opts: Modern cryptography and a minimal codebase
exp: Tiny audited codebase + fast modern crypto (ChaCha20-Poly1305).

mcqs.q: Which statement about proxy firewalls is TRUE?
opts: They terminate and re-originate connections per protocol
exp: The intermediary break gives real content awareness at the cost of speed.

mcqs.q: Egress filtering primarily prevents:
exp: Exit-point control stops exfiltration and outbound abuse (also anti-spam hygiene).

mcqs.q: SSL/TLS VPNs traverse corporate firewalls easily because they:
opts: Look like ordinary HTTPS on port 443
exp: Indistinguishable from normal web traffic to most filters.

mcqs.q: Which rule matches the traffic 'any web browsing TO server 2.2.2.2'?
exp: Web = tcp/80; extended ACL grammar with eq 80.

mcqs.q: A 'personal firewall' runs:
opts: On an end host, controlling its own traffic
exp: Host-based layer of defense in depth.

mcqs.q: Which is a REASON to segment with an internal firewall (not just at the edge)?
opts: Limit lateral movement after a breach
exp: Internal segmentation contains breaches - the zero-trust instinct.

mcqs.q: IPsec site-to-site tunnels terminate typically on:
exp: Gateway-to-gateway: the tunnels connect the networks, not individual hosts.

mcqs.q: Which firewall feature stops an employee tunneling forbidden apps over port 443?
exp: DPI identifies the true application regardless of port.

mcqs.q: The wildcard mask 0.0.0.63 corresponds to prefix:
Which is a HOST-based firewall example?
exp: Runs on the endpoint itself - last line of defense in depth.

mcqs.q: Stateful failover pairs of firewalls provide:
exp: State synchronisation keeps sessions alive through a device failure.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE about the DMZ and the LAN?
opts: DMZ systems compromise should not grant LAN access
exp: Zoning exists precisely so a public-facing breach stops at the DMZ.

mcqs.q: An 'implicit deny' means:
opts: Traffic not matched by any rule is dropped
exp: The invisible final rule of every serious ACL.

mcqs.q: A published AXIS PYQ permits SMTP to only 1.1.1.1. Why must the ACL be EXTENDED (100-199)?
opts: Standard ACLs cannot filter by protocol/destination port
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: eq smtp = port filtering = extended-only capability; standard lists see source IPs alone.

mcqs.q: An attacker sends packets with the ACK flag set for a session that never existed. Which firewall drops them first?
exp: No state entry for the ACK -> dropped; header-only filters would pass it.

mcqs.q: Which design places the DMZ between TWO firewalls, inside and outside?
exp: The two-device sandwich - strongest classic perimeter topology.

mcqs.q: IPsec tunnel mode between gateways: the inner header visible after decryption belongs to:
exp: Tunnel mode preserves the original endpoints inside; the outer header is gateway-to-gateway.

mcqs.q: Why does ESP alone usually replace AH+ESP in NAT environments?
opts: AH authenticates immutable header fields that NAT rewrites
exp: NAT changes IPs/ports -> AH's integrity check fails; ESP's coverage survives NAT (with NAT-T).

mcqs.q: A NGFW shows 'TeamViewer' on port 443. Which capability produced that label?
exp: Payload signatures identify the true application regardless of port - generation-4 capability.

mcqs.q: Split tunnelling in a remote-access VPN means:
opts: Internet traffic goes direct; corporate traffic goes through the tunnel
All traffic is forced through the tunnel
exp: Convenience vs security trade-off: full-tunnel forces everything through corporate inspection.

mcqs.q: An ACL must block telnet TO a server while allowing SSH. Correct pair:
opts: deny tcp any host S eq 23 + permit tcp any host S eq 22
exp: 23 = telnet (block), 22 = SSH (allow) - explicit rules, order matters (first match wins).

mcqs.q: A stateful firewall survives a reboot without dropping sessions because of:
opts: State synchronisation to its failover peer
exp: Clustered firewalls replicate the state table - high availability.

mcqs.q: Which statement comparing proxy and NGFW is TRUE?
opts: Proxies terminate connections per protocol; NGFW inspects inline across applications
exp: Explicit intermediary vs inline transparent inspection - the architectural difference.

mcqs.q: An ACL permits 'tcp any host 1.1.1.1 eq smtp' but the mail flow still fails. First thing to check:
opts: The RETURN traffic (ephemeral source ports) - stateful inspection or a reply rule
exp: Mail servers reply FROM port 25 TO ephemeral client ports - return-path rules or state handling must cover it.

mcqs.q: Which VPN flaw makes PPTP unacceptable?
opts: Broken encryption (MS-CHAPv2 cracks) and no modern integrity
exp: Cryptographically broken for years - the canonical 'insecure legacy VPN' answer.

mcqs.q: A company wants remote access WITHOUT installing clients and WITHOUT exposing RDP/SSH to the Internet. Best fit:
opts: IPsec tunnel mode to every laptop
exp: SSL-VPN portals proxy internal apps over 443 - no client, no exposed management ports.

mcqs.q: Which firewall generation first introduced CONNECTION CONTEXT?
exp: The state table is generation 3's invention - replies judged by session membership.

mcqs.q: An any-any-permit firewall with logging is equivalent security-wise to:
exp: Permit-everything enforces no policy - logging alone is observation, not control.

mcqs.q: Which IPsec piece prevents REPLAY of captured tunnel packets?
exp: Anti-replay windows use per-packet sequence numbers inside ESP/AH.

mcqs.q: A DMZ web server is compromised. Which architecture detail limits the blast radius to the DMZ?
opts: Rules denying DMZ-initiated connections into the LAN
exp: Zoning works only if DMZ->LAN flows are denied by default - the whole point of the segment.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct wildcard for permitting the 10.1.16.0/24 network in an ACL?
NGFW user-based policies require:
opts: Identity integration (directory/SSO) so rules apply per USER not per IP
exp: Generation-4 policies bind to users/groups - identity feeds the firewall.

mcqs.q: Order these perimeter designs weakest to strongest:
opts: Screened router, screened host, three-legged DMZ, screened subnet
exp: One filter -> filter+bastion -> one box three zones -> two boxes sandwiching: monotonic strength.
